summary: This informational memo is an introductory guide to common TCP/IP and Internet tools and utilities. It also covers discussion lists, ways to obtain Internet documents, and resources for finding your way around the Internet.

eli5.summary: A beginner's toolbox guide for exploring the Internet.

subtitle: A mid-1990s beginner's tour of ping, traceroute, telnet, FTP, Gopher, the Web, mailing lists and how to find RFCs.

tldr.problem: New Internet users in the 1990s had many tools and services available but no single plain guide to what each one did or how to use it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo walks through the common TCP/IP utilities one by one, with real sample sessions, then covers information servers, the Web, discussion lists and newsgroups, and where to get Internet documents.
tldr.outcome: It is a snapshot of the 1997 toolbox, written as a self-study tutorial or lab manual. It replaces RFC 1739 and is also FYI 30.

today: RFC 2151 is an Informational memo, also FYI 30, and it obsoletes RFC 1739. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes it; the tools and sites it describes reflect 1997, and the memo says security issues are not discussed in it.

sections.title: Purpose and Conventions
sections.content:
RFC 2151 is an introductory guide to many of the most commonly available TCP/IP and Internet tools and utilities, from checking whether a host is up to viewing a multimedia thesis. It also covers discussion lists, ways to obtain Internet documents and resources that help users find their way around. The authors say it can serve as a tutorial for self-learning, a step-by-step laboratory manual for a course, or the basis of a site's users manual. It is a basic guide only and points elsewhere for detail.

The sample sessions came from several systems, including AIX on an IBM RS/6000, Linux on an Intel 486, Multinet TCP/IP over VMS on a VAX, and FTP Software's OnNet on a DOS/Windows PC. The memo warns that not every utility exists on every host and that interfaces differ. It deliberately shows text sessions rather than Windows ones, because graphical packages hide the detail needed to understand what really happens. In command syntax, square brackets mark optional items and a vertical bar means "or".
sections.eli5: It is a how-to book for a toolbox. The authors tried every tool on different computers and wrote down exactly what they saw.

sections.title: Finding Out About Hosts and Domains
sections.content:
Four tools tell you about hosts and domains. NSLOOKUP queries the Domain Name System: given a name it returns the address, and the other way round. By default it looks at address records, but set type=MX asks for mail exchange records, and the example shows mail for one domain tried in order of a preference value.

Ping sends ICMP Echo messages to see whether a host is active and to measure round-trip delay. The default is 56 data bytes, giving a 64 byte packet, and the memo shows options for count, wait, packet size and quiet output. Finger reports who is logged in on another system, or details about one user, as described in RFC 1288.

Traceroute shows the route packets take. The original version sends UDP datagrams to an invalid port with the TTL set to 1, then 2, and so on. Each router that sees an expired datagram returns an ICMP Time Exceeded message, and the final host's Destination Unreachable reply tells the program it has arrived. Defaults are 30 hops maximum, 3 probes per TTL, a 5 second wait and port 33434. The memo notes it began as a quick debugging aid for a routing problem.
sections.eli5: Ping is shouting "hello?" down a hallway to see if anyone answers. Traceroute is asking each door along the hallway to say its name as you walk past.

sections.title: TELNET and FTP
sections.content:
The memo calls TELNET and the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) the two fundamental tools, dating back to the early ARPANET. TELNET is TCP/IP's virtual terminal protocol: a user logs in to a remote host as if on a directly attached terminal. Giving a port number turns it into a general client, so telnet host_name 79 can stand in for a missing Finger client. Other well-known TCP ports it lists are 25 for SMTP, 43 for whois, 80 for HTTP and 119 for NNTP.

FTP moves files between hosts. Anonymous FTP lets users fetch files from archive sites without an account, using the username anonymous. Historically the password was guest, though most systems by then asked for an e-mail address. The memo stresses setting the transfer type to image (binary) for executables, and describes dir, cd, get, put, close and quit. TELNET would give full access to the remote system, whereas FTP limits the user to file transfer.
sections.eli5: TELNET lets you sit at another computer's keyboard from far away. FTP is like a delivery truck that carries files to you or takes them to someone else.

sections.title: Finding People and Information
sections.content:
For finding users the memo describes WHOIS/NICNAME, which searches databases for network and system administrators, RFC authors and other registered contacts (the protocol is in RFC 954), and KNOWBOT, a service that queries several user databases at once.

For finding files and documents it describes a family of early information servers. Archie, developed in 1992 at McGill University, indexes files at anonymous FTP sites and refreshes each registered site about once a month; the memo says it was no longer as popular as before. Gopher, developed at the University of Minnesota in 1991 and described in RFC 1436, organizes information in simple menus and links sites together. VERONICA and JUGHEAD add keyword searching of Gopher menus, and WAIS offers one interface to many databases.

Each tool is shown through TELNET sessions, since the book is meant to work even if a local client is missing.
sections.eli5: Before search engines, people used phone-book style lists and library card catalogs for the Internet. These tools were those catalogs.

sections.title: The Web, Lists and Newsgroups
sections.content:
The World Wide Web was developed in the early 1990s at CERN in Geneva. It treats files as hypertext and lets one client reach text, sound, images, animation and video. The memo says that by early 1996 the Web accounted for over 40% of Internet traffic. Users run a browser and point it at a Uniform Resource Locator (URL), which can name HTTP, FTP, Gopher or TELNET resources. It credits Mosaic, from NCSA in 1994, as the first widely used browser, and shows the text browser Lynx. Many of the earlier tools were reachable through Web pages, which act as a viewer for a remote client.

For conversation, the memo explains unmoderated and moderated discussion lists, the convention of sending administrative requests to a separate request address rather than the list, and the list servers LISTSERV and Majordomo. Usenet newsgroups use the Network News Transfer Protocol, and their names are hierarchical, with mainstream and alternative hierarchies.
sections.eli5: The Web is a giant book where words can jump you to other pages. Mailing lists and newsgroups are clubs where people with the same hobby write to each other.

sections.title: Internet Documentation
sections.content:
The memo introduces the document series. RFCs hold protocols, standards, research questions, hot topics, humor (especially those dated 1 April) and general information. An RFC number is never reused; a revised document gets a new number and the old one is said to be obsoleted. STD numbers mark Internet standards and always refer to the latest version, so UDP is identified as STD-6/RFC-768. FYI documents explain topics for the wide range of Internet users, and the memo also covers Best Current Practices.

It explains how to fetch these documents by e-mail servers, anonymous FTP and Web sites, with a sample retrieval of RFC 1594. The standards process itself is described in RFC 2026. The memo ends with pointers for further exploration and a list of acronyms.
sections.eli5: RFCs are the Internet's rule books and notes. Once a number is used it is never given to another book, and a new edition gets a new number.
